 {"list":[{"chapter_code":"DEU28","exceeding":[{"verses":"31","findings":[{"word":"מוֹשִֽׁיעַ׃","parsing":"Verb - Hifil - Participle - masculine singular","term":"perfect","elsewhere":[],"explain":"The action word for saving, in the stem that means making someone or something else do the action, in the describing form that turns an action into the one doing it, masculine and one of it. A rescuer. Verse twenty-nine ended with these same words, and this one adds two letters: for you. There is no one saving — for you. The line has got closer. Look at what this verse is actually built out of. Three animals, and every farm in the country had them: the ox that ploughs, the donkey that carries, the flock that clothes and feeds. Between them they are a family's work, its transport and its savings. And each one goes in a different way, so that no comfort is left standing. The ox is killed in front of the man — he sees it happen. The donkey is dragged off and simply never comes back — he does not see where it went. The flock is handed over to people he knows are his enemies — he knows exactly where it is and cannot go and get it. Watched, vanished, and known about. That is every way there is to lose a thing. And notice the small cruelty in the first line, because it is the sharpest thing here. The ox is butchered — the kitchen word, the word for making dinner — and the man does not eat any of it. The smell of his own meat cooking, and none of it his. It is a whole life reduced to standing still while things are done in front of you. Which is the same picture as the man groping at noon two verses ago: a person who can see perfectly well and can do nothing at all. Look at what this verse is actually built out of. Three animals, and every farm in the country had them: the ox that ploughs, the donkey that carries, the flock that clothes and feeds. Between them they are a family's work, its transport and its savings. And each one goes in a different way, so that no comfort is left standing. The ox is killed in front of the man — he sees it happen. The donkey is dragged off and simply never comes back — he does not see where it went. The flock is handed over to people he knows are his enemies — he knows exactly where it is and cannot go and get it. Watched, vanished, and known about. That is every way there is to lose a thing. And notice the small cruelty in the first line, because it is the sharpest thing here. The ox is butchered — the kitchen word, the word for making dinner — and the man does not eat any of it. The smell of his own meat cooking, and none of it his. It is a whole life reduced to standing still while things are done in front of you.
